plymouth.name: Omarchy Matrix
plymouth.description: Omarchy's splash with the line from the start of the film.
plymouth.//lines: What is typed BEFORE the passphrase is answered, in order. Knock is last on purpose: in the film it lands with the knock at Neo's door, and here it lands with the prompt. `afterUnlock` below types once the passphrase is accepted.
//afterUnlock: What is typed AFTER the passphrase is accepted, once boot proceeds.
The derived script holds the storyboard at the end of `lines` while a
passphrase dialog is up, and releases it from the unlock callback -- so
on an encrypted disk this line only ever starts once the disk is open.
On a disk with no passphrase there is no dialog to wait for, and the
storyboard simply plays through. Empty or absent keeps the old shape:
the boot lines, then progress, with no held gate.
//modes: What is typed on the way OUT, keyed by the mode plymouthd was started
with -- which is what the theme's `Plymouth.GetMode()` reports. `boot` is
`lines` above; anything named here replaces it for that mode only.
THERE ARE ONLY TWO EXITS, not three. `plymouth-halt.service`,
a halt cannot be told apart from a power off from inside the script, and
a `halt` key here would be config that never runs.
The exits are SHORT: the splash lives until the machine does, which is a
couple of seconds. Only the first line is reliably seen, so the first line
is the payoff -- see EXIT_PACE in lib/derive-plymouth.py, which types
these faster and holds them for less than the boot's.
Shutdown answers the boot: it opens by waking Mr. Anderson and closes by
saying goodbye to him, and `Unplug him.` is what is actually happening.
Reboot is the film's own definition of one -- a deja vu is a glitch in the
Matrix, and it happens when they change something.
//color: The typed lines' CORE colour, r, g, b in 0..1. Used to be absent on
purpose, so the lines took the theme's own `green` from colors.toml --
but that green is deliberately yellow-leaning (see colors.toml's own
comment), and next to the film's own stills the typed lines read as
swamp rather than as a monitor.
MEASURED, not chosen: the brightest pixel cluster (the CORE of a typed
line, where the phosphor overexposes toward white) sat within a few
points of RGB 170/208/194 across four separate reference frames --
consistently pale and blue-leaning, not the saturated green people
remember the effect as. #AAD0C2 is that average.
The core and the glow are NOT the same colour any more -- see
glowColor below for why -- so `color` alone no longer reproduces the
old single-colour look. Omit both to fall back to the old behaviour.
//glowColor: The bloom AROUND a typed line, a different colour from the core on
purpose: in the reference stills the centre of the ink overexposes to
near-white (`color` above) while the halo a few pixels out is a
saturated, blue-leaning green -- two colours, not one colour at two
opacities. A single blur of the core alone cannot reproduce that; see
the comment above LINE_GLOW_BLUR in derive-plymouth.py.
MEASURED the same way as `color`: the halo's own mid-brightness band,
sampled well away from the core, sat around a 1:8:5 R:G:B ratio --
green with blue riding well above red, not the accent's yellow lean.
#22D68C keeps that ratio at a brightness the blur math already assumes.
Omit it and the glow is baked from `color` instead -- one colour for

//titles: In the panel's filled title band, the way an old window manager
captioned a window. The panel wears one of FOUR of these at a time --
these two, and the grantedText/deniedText below -- and swaps the whole
baked band rather than composing a frame and a caption at boot.
//grantedDenied: The one-shot feedback, worn by the title band itself -- not layered
over the content row underneath it. Both were tried in that row first,
under a band that still said `enter password` or the progress title, and
that is two captions saying the same thing in two places at once.
ACCESS GRANTED plays once, the moment the passphrase is accepted, then
the band hands over to progressTitle and the real progress track.
